# Data description 

This is a movie and entertainment dataset from the dataset platform Kaggle. According to CourseEra, Kaggle is a platform where data science and machine learning experts can compete and develop models for problem solving. It also provides access to notebooks and skill tutorials. Kaggle offers a wide and diverse range of datasets and machine learning models, all you have to do is search up the topic you are interested in studying and Kaggle will pull up a list of related datasets. That is how I found this movie dataset, because I knew I was interested in doing my final project on entertainment data. https://www.coursera.org/articles/kaggle, https://www.kaggle.com/ 

Moving on to the movie dataset specifically, it includes detailed data for 916 modern feature films from between January 2024 and December 2026. There are 20 total data attributes, all of them individual records, such as movie titles, release dates, genres, audience/critic ratings (out of 10),  vote counts, run times, production budgets, worldwide box office revenue, directors, writers, cast, production studios, content ratings, language, country of origin, plot synopses, and more. Scrolling down, I see that the maker of this dataset collected data from Wikipedia Open API & Public Film Catalogs, Wikipedia OpenSearch API and Unsplash Media, a high-quality film poster website.

As I mentioned above, this dataset contains information on 20 different attributes for each of the 916 films included. The categories range from runtime to audience rating to box office earnings. The time period it covers is January 2024 to December 2026, as it contains some information for movies that have been made but not yet released to the general public. For the sake of my analysis, I plan to take out unreleased movies from this dataset since there might be some misleading or missing data for them. 

The two hypotheses I plan to test are: 
1. Higher production budgets correspond with higher audience ratings.
2. Longer run times correspond with higher audience ratings. 

For this reason, the columns that will be most important to my analysis are "rating_out_of_10," "budget_usd" and "runtime_minutes." Also "title," of course. After examining the data, I can see that there are 29 films coming out in either November or December 2026. Some of them might have come out in the first couple weeks of November, meaning I could include them in my analysis, but I would need to do some deeper digging because there is a lot of missing data for the exact "release_day" category, even for movies that came out in 2024. This is something I might want to keep an eye or on investigate further. I will also actively have to keep track of when upcoming movies are released as we get closer to the due date for our final project. Perhaps to make things easier I will pick a day in the near future when I do my most thorough analysis of the data and use that as my cut off line, even if more movies get released between then and the project due date. I don't want my findings to be constantly changing. 

Professor Willis let me know that budget figures are often missing in movie data, so I took his advice and looked through the dataset for missing budgets. First to rule out any $0 figures, I set the "budget_usd" column so that the lowest numbers came to the top. I found no $0 budgets. Then I scrolled through and looked for any "NA" inputs, also finding none. It looks like all 916 movies included in this dataset have budget data attached to them. However, here is where a whole different problem arose. The lowest value in the dataset is $10,849,306 for the 2025 horror/thriller movie "Ash." Yeah. I immediately became concerned, because that figure seemed way to high for a random movie I had never heard of. Plus, if this was supposed to be the lowest figure in the dataset, that was even more concerning. After a quick Google search, I discovered that Ash's production budget was closer to $500,000. Moving on, the maximum production budget value listed in this dataset is $171,246,357 for the July 2026 movie "Descendants: Wicked Wonderland." First of all, no movie has a budget that high. Second of all, if a movie were to have a budget that high, I can almost guarantee that it would not be in the Descendants franchise. This is data is definitely not accurate, and my findings led me to examine other categories of data more closely. Some of the data does look correct, such as release dates, genres, and names of directors and screenwriters. But the number categories all seem way, way off. Aside from the production budget category, the box office category is also completely false. This dataset claims "Descendants: Wicked Wonderland" earned $510,700,365 at the box office, yet this movie did not even come out in theaters. It debuted on streaming platforms, meaning it had no box office earnings to make. Even the run times aren't really correct.

This is a big bummer, because I was really excited to find this data. I definitely should have taken a deeper look at the data sooner. However, the non-number data in the dataset still seems to be correct, so I could potentially pivot my assignment to explore a different movie-related relationship. For example, I could look at how movie genres and audience ratings correlate. My hypothesis could be that romance movies tend to score higher audience ratings, or alternatively, that sci-fi films tend to score lower audience ratings.
